zh_summary: @jasonfurman on the Bank Fund meetings in Bangkok: the words are all negative but the numbers positive, with the IMF upgrading its forecast, and no one cares about tariffs anymore.
en_summary: @jasonfurman on the Bank Fund meetings in Bangkok: the words are all negative but the numbers positive, with the IMF upgrading its forecast, and no one cares about tariffs anymore.
text:
Some impressions from the Bank-Fund meetings in Bangkok:

1. The words are all negative but the numbers are all positive. Is all about unprecedented waves of shocks and risks while the IMF upgraded the forecast to something even stronger.

2. No one cares about tariffs anymore, they expect them to continue forever and have adjusted and moved on.

3. Everyone cares a lot about high interest rates. They expect them to continue forever but they haven't moved on.

4. Oil prices fall somewhere between these two. Everyone cares some, aren't sure if they'll continue and have partially moved on.

5. Everyone is having exactly the same conversations about AI as they are having here: will the demand boost continue, is it a bubble, will it kill jobs, when will it show up in productivity. I sensed much more optimism than pessimism and finance ministers and central bankers are not particuarly interested in p(doom).

6. No one seemed to mind that Scott Bessent didn't bother to attend.

"The cost of borrowing against your stocks just went up by 25 bps. How much are stocks up by this year?"

"The increase of the debt of the carrying costs has become a rounding error compared to the upside of the underlying position that loan is financing. It's similar to the dynamic we see with Bitcoin-backed loans."

"A Bitcoin-backed loan interest rate at Ledn starts at 9.25%. Anybody that took a loan from Ledn at 9.25% when Bitcoin was at 65 or 70 has seen the value of that collateral increase by 25 to 35%."

"As long as the cost of financing the debt is a fraction of the price action of the asset that debt is financing, we're still very much in the clear in terms of those ratios and that dynamic."

"Every single person at Ledn today, even at a $500 loan, can borrow at lower interest than what Strategy's paying on their preferreds. The smallest loan at Ledn is 11.49%. STRC yields are at 12% right now."

name: Cullen Roche
zh_summary: @cullenroche: MMTers misread reserve accounting; total Fed remittances matter, not IORB alone, and the Fed's recent operating losses have been net stimulative versus prior years' large remittances.
en_summary: @cullenroche: MMTers misread reserve accounting; total Fed remittances matter, not IORB alone, and the Fed's recent operating losses have been net stimulative versus prior years' large remittances.
text:
It’s becoming clear that MMTers have a worse understanding of reserve accounting than we thought. 

What matters is the total remittances, not IORB in isolation. And yes, in recent years the Fed has been operating at a loss, which has been net stimulative relative to the large positive remittances of prior years even though this income effect was offset by the tighter credit conditions that accompanied the rate hikes, which were a clear net drag and help explain why inflation fell after 2022.

What’s even more off-base about the idea that this might cause inflation is that the remittances matter in rate of change, not just levels. Saying “there’s $500B of new income because of IORB” doesn’t mean we got inflation from it. If you got $100B every year for 5 years you don’t get ongoing inflation because the rate of change isn’t changing. And in recent years the net interest impact has been improving as the Fed’s annual losses have shrunk substantially, meaning the incremental addition to the consolidated government deficit from this channel has been getting smaller, not larger. They have the direction of the flow backwards and this exercise explains why their theory of inflation has been so wrong in recent years.

Matt discusses the current situation but I think It’s really about going forward.  If new unsecured debt in the AI space is being priced at 15%, that’s basically saying capital isn’t going to fund these companies again.  So the companies that are bleeding cash will have to use equity to finance 2-3 more years of operating losses and severely dilute current shareholders.  Yes the projects and chips may survive but that may end up being owned by the securitized debt holders and equity may get wrecked in the process.   Now on top of that you’re seeing secured debt getting priced at 10% now too (see FT article).  Add on some delays, political pushback, permitting issues, and investor concerns about risks and you can run into a situation where private equity doesn’t get paid back anytime soon.  So it’s not “panic”, it’s repricing.  And the reprice may not be so great.   This benefits the companies that are financing a lot of their capex via legacy free cash flow.  The debt heavy new incumbents may have problems.

text:

@robin_j_brooks is right to highlight the IRGC's impact on freight, but the bigger story is market fragmentation. name: jeroen blokland
zh_summary: @jsblokland: investing revolves around nominal returns, yet after one of the worst bond bear markets you must go back 30 years to find a positive cumulative real return on bonds.
en_summary: @jsblokland: investing revolves around nominal returns, yet after one of the worst bond bear markets you must go back 30 years to find a positive cumulative real return on bonds.
text:
It is rather remarkable that nearly everything in investing revolves around nominal returns.

Institutional investors determine their strategic asset allocation largely on the basis of nominal data.

Following one of the worst bond bear markets on record, you now have to go back 30 years to find a positive cumulative real return on bonds.

Many investors simply do not realize that three decades of real returns from bond investing have effectively been wiped out.

That does not mean bonds cannot perform well from here, especially now that real yields have turned positive again.

But if you were to use real returns in a standard mean-variance optimization model, as most institutional investors do, there is virtually no chance that bonds would receive an allocation anywhere near 40% in the strategic asset mix.

In fact, bonds receive no allocation at all once you expand the investment universe beyond different types of stocks and bonds.

And the outlook for bonds, something that is almost never incorporated into traditional mean-variance optimization models, becomes significantly less attractive when you factor in the prospect of higher inflation.
